issues.span:
Regarding impurity and so forth,
That is false, like the convention of purity and so forth.
issues.evidence: Tibetan: དེ་ནི་མི་གཙང་ལ་སོགས་ལ། གཙང་སོགས་གྲགས་པ་བཞིན་དུ་རྫུན། The phrase 'regarding impurity' (མི་གཙང་ལ་སོགས་ལ) belongs with the convention of purity (གཙང་སོགས་གྲགས་པ), as bo-kunpal 9-6 shows (the body of a woman is impure, yet is conventionally called pure). The English attaches it to 'That is false', so 'purity regarding impurity' is lost.
issues.fix:
That is false, just as the convention of purity and so forth
regarding impure things and so forth is false.

issues.span:
Merit from a Victor like an illusion
Is just as it is for one who is truly existent.
issues.evidence: Tibetan ཇི་ལྟར ('how?') in line 2 is the opponent's question, and ཇི་བཞིན ('just as') is the reply. bo-gyaltsab 9-9 and bo-kunpal 9-9 read the pair as objection plus answer. The English drops 'how' and gives only a flat statement, with no marking that the first part is the objection and the second part the reply.
issues.fix:
"How is there merit from a Victor like an illusion?"
[Reply:] Just as it is for one who is truly existent.

issues.span: because it is seen by one endowed with other conditions
issues.evidence: Tibetan རྐྱེན་གཞན་དག་དང་ལྡན་པ་ནི། མཐོང་ཕྱིར: the one endowed with other conditions is the one who sees, namely other persons' minds. bo-kunpal 9-24 says those so endowed see the minds of other persons (གང་ཟག་གཞན་གྱི་སེམས་དག་ཀྱང་མཐོང་བའི་ཕྱིར), so one's own mind, which is nearer, should be luminous. bo-shenga 9-24 says the same. The English makes the mind 'it' the thing seen by such a person, which reverses agent and object.
issues.fix:
If, because one endowed with other conditions sees [others' minds],
it is luminous to itself,
